title: How agents broke app-level infrastructure - Evan Boyle
talk_summary: Evan Boyle argues that agentic workflows break assumptions of web-era infra: multi-minute runtimes, bursty rate limits, provider outages, and non-resumable serverless timeouts.

takeaways.technique: API/compute plane separation with stream-based state
takeaways.what_they_do: The API layer invokes compute once, passing a Redis stream ID; all status and output are read from that stream, so the API never talks to the compute layer again and clients can reconnect and resume.
takeaways.evidence_quote: The API layer invokes the compute layer and passes it in a reddish stream ID. That's the last time that the API layer is going to have to talk to the compute layer.
as the sandbox program executes, it's going to emit heartbeats so that the background processes within the system can monitor and make sure that a workflow runs to completion

takeaways.what_they_do: Each reusable, idempotent component gets its own retry boundary and error boundary, configurable via a fluent API (e.g., exponential backoff with a retry count) so only the failing step retries, not the whole workflow.
takeaways.evidence_quote: every single step, we're going to get a retry boundary, an error boundary off each component

takeaways.what_they_do: They structure agents as small idempotent steps that can be run and tested in isolation, then composed into workflows, explicitly avoiding heavy abstraction.
takeaways.evidence_quote: components that are reusable, item potent, independently testable steps and then workflows that are collections of components that run together

takeaways.what_they_do: When workflows can run 60 minutes, they explicitly design worker draining and blue-green deployment so in-flight runs aren't killed by a deploy.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If you're going to let your workflows run for 60 minutes, you have to be very very careful about how you drain workers

takeaways.technique: Assume provider outages and bursty limits; design for failover
takeaways.what_they_do: He shows correlated outages across OpenAI and Gemini and bursty traffic patterns, arguing rate limits and downtime must be treated as normal, not exceptional.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we have an outage during the exact same time period. And even if you don't hit an outage, you still have rate limits to contend with.
